title: How to Read a Pool Tournament Bracket: Single vs Double Elimination Explained
description: New to pool tournaments? Learn how single and double elimination brackets work, what a race to 7 and hill-hill mean, and how to follow your path.
body:
You walk into a pool hall on tournament night, and there it is: a big sheet of paper covered in lines, names and numbers. Everyone seems to know where to look. If you have ever stared at a bracket and wondered whether you were winning, losing or just lost, this guide is for you.

Once you can read a bracket, every tournament gets easier to enjoy, whether you are entering your first local event or watching the pros. Here is the plain-English version.

What is a tournament bracket?

A bracket is a map of who plays whom, and in what order. Each line is a path. Win your match and your name moves along the line to the next round. Keep winning and you reach the final at the far end.

Most pool events use one of two main styles: single elimination or double elimination.

Single elimination: win or go home

This is the simplest bracket. Lose once and you are out. It is quick, easy to follow and popular for small fields or short events.

  • Round 1: players are paired up. Winners advance.
  • Round 2 and beyond: winners meet winners until two players are left.
  • Final: the last two play for the title.

With 8 players you need 3 rounds. With 16 you need 4. Each extra round doubles the size of the field it can handle.

Double elimination: a second chance

Most local and pro pool tournaments use double elimination, because one bad rack should not end your day. You are knocked out only after your second loss.

The bracket splits into two sides:

  • Winners side (the "front side"): everyone starts here. Win and you stay.
  • Loser side (the "back side"): lose once and you drop here. From now on, any loss sends you home.

The winner of the loser side then plays the undefeated winners-side player in the final. Rules for the last match vary by event. In many events the player coming from the loser side has to win twice, since they already have one loss. Always check the event rules posted at the venue or online.

What is a "race to"?

You will often see something like "race to 7." That means the first player to win 7 games wins the match. A longer race rewards consistency. A shorter race gives underdogs more chances.

Different rounds can have different race lengths. Early rounds are often shorter, and the semi-finals and final are often longer.

Hill-hill: the most exciting two words in pool

"Hill" means one game away from winning the match. When both players are on the hill, that is "hill-hill," and the next game decides everything. In a race to 7, hill-hill means the score is 6-6.

It is the pool version of a final-minute goal. Crowds usually gather around the table.

Seeding and the draw

Some brackets are seeded, meaning the strongest players are placed so they do not meet too early. Others are a blind draw, where names are picked at random. A blind draw is common at friendly local events because everyone has a fair shot at a favorable path.

Byes: a free pass

If the number of players does not fit neatly into the bracket, some players get a "bye," which means they skip a round without playing. It is not a bad thing or a reward for bad play. It is simply math. A bye lets the rest of the bracket line up evenly.

How to follow your path in four steps

  1. Find your name in round 1.
  2. Look at the line to the right. That is where you go if you win.
  3. In double elimination, look for the loser-side line too. That is where you go if you lose.
  4. Note your table number and ask the tournament director when to be ready. Many events call matches out loud, so stay close.

Where team events fit in

Not every event uses a bracket. The Mosconi Cup, for example, is a team event where Team USA and Team Europe score points across sessions rather than knocking players out. If you want to see how that works, read our Mosconi Cup format explained and the Mosconi Cup 2026 hub. The 2026 event is scheduled for November 27 to 30 at the Caribe Royale in Orlando, Florida.

Find an event and try it

The best way to learn brackets is to play in one. Browse the tournament finder, check the calendar for dates near you, or see what is on in the this weekend list. Before you go, read our pool etiquette guide so you know the unwritten rules, and keep our pool terms glossary handy for the slang.

Quick tips for your first bracket

  • Arrive early and check in so your name is on the bracket.
  • Ask what the race lengths are before you start.
  • Know the rules being played, such as 8-ball or 9-ball, and any local variations.
  • Do not worry about losing early. In double elimination, you often get another match.
  • Be a good sport. Shake hands after every match.

That is all there is to it. Lines, rounds, a race to a number, and the thrill of hill-hill. See you at the tables.
